utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was not important at the time. If a village came under attack, all the villages voluntarily offered to help. So, for example, when the attack began on Jabllanice I asked for assistance from other villages, because Ramush could not come from Gllogjan to the place where I was. So whichever village was able to send volunteers to help, they would do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What you appear to be describing is a fairly horizontal, rather than vertical, command structure. Would you accept that description?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's what happened. It's something that really happened. Whichever villages were closer to where the attack occurred, those villages went to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in your witness statement at paragraph 68 you explain a line of reporting. You say: "I reported to Nazif Ramabaja," who was the commander of your brigade, I believe, "who, in turn, reported to Tahir Zemaj and Ramush Haradinaj." Is that how you understood it, that Nazif Ramabaja may report to Tahir Zemaj, he may report to Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood the situation to be. When we came back from the front line, we discussed what had occurred, what we had done. But the reporting did not occur immediately after something happened. Sometimes it also occurred weeks after. But our attempts were towards creating an army, to have a General Staff, and a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But those attempts at this stage were in a fairly rudimentary and early stage of their development. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always tried, even earlier, but we could not do it because we did not have the means and there were attacks every day. So we never had a proper command, a Joint Command or staff. Because every country in the world has a General Staff that commands in times of war, while in our case each village had a staff. So it means that we were more than one country, we were several countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's a fairly chaotic picture that you're painting of the organisation. Is that right? Is that how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very correct. Only if you compare the means that we had at our disposal with the means that the Serbs had. They had planes, tanks, while we only had Kalashnikovs. So this is a comparison that is beyond comparison. But the will of the young people, that is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you in that context how easy it was to impose discipline on young volunteers in practical terms, how easy it was to control the actions of the young volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has listened now for quite some time to testimony which covers ground similar to what we've heard already.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quite a lot of times and this next question, how easy it was, I mean, it could be very easy or not very easy, that of course is not very factual. It's -- and a lot of these testimonies, as they were in the past, give a mixture of facts and opinions --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I don't know whether it's the best use of our time --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to hear these kind of mixtures from every witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's a picture of command arrangements and if Your Honour feels the position is adequately covered, then I'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Albeit a connected one, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In your witness statement at paragraph 66, you describe Ramush having visited your brigade two or three times in total during the period of time that you were stationed at Baran. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Over a period of approximately two months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you say that he was on the move a lot. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a different question that I was asked. Of course people move, but at the time he came to our zone three times. He tried -- and we all tried to have somebody to go to places so that we could have things under control. But we could not achieve that, because if a village came under attack, he was the one to respond first.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The specific question, I think you may have started to answer it towards the end of your answer, the specific question I'm asking you is: Was it your understanding that Mr. Haradinaj was constantly moving around?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that if he went to a village, the morale in that village was boosted. So I don't know how often he moved --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and what means he had to move, but whenever he had the time and the possibility, he went places, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Can I ask you, please, in the light of that answer about an answer you gave yesterday. You were asked by Mr. Re about what feedback you may have heard from people about his command style. And your answer was this: "Ramush had no time to command everywhere, but people trusted him. They thought that if Ramush was there, there would be no problem for them, for the people. This is something that occurred among the people, that's how the people loved him." And I just wanted to ask you this: What did you mean by that comment "Ramush had no time to command everywhere ..."?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The front line was about 50 kilometres long, and we did not have or he did not have any means or communication means. Even if you had the modern means of communication, it would be difficult to command all the front line that I described. He probably went to Dubrave, Gramaqel, or Prilep, but the Lugu i Baranit villages remained without anyone because we did not have another Ramush. So he could not command all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now let me move, if I may please, on to some of the evidence that you've given, both in witness statements and in maps and in your testimony, about Serb deployments because there, I think, was a point yesterday where we moved from one map to another and you realised that there was information that you had left off one of the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we bring up, please, P355. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to understand a little bit more about this picture first of all. It's not, obviously, got details of topographical features like hills and mountains marked on it, but you told us yesterday that as a general practice the Serb forces were occupying high ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, can I just ask you some specific questions of clarification arising out of both your statements and some of the answers that you've given. I'm looking at this blue area shown on this map. First of all, is it right that there were Serb forces stationed on Suka Cermjan, on the eastern side of Lake Radoniq?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were there and all along the dam, and they were in the Lake Radoniq area.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What dam are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the dam of the Lake Radoniq, and then Suka i Biteshit and then the main road Gjakove-Decan-Baballoq village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear then, do you know from what period of time there were Serb forces located on Suka Cermjan, from when to when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces entered there in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were they there throughout the summer?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed there until the villages fell. They were on the higher ground points. They observed the villages from those higher points and shelled the villages from there. Those were strategic points. There is the Pulaj village there, the Decan clinic or Podi i Geshtenjave where the heavy artillery was stationed, heavy calibre artillery, and from there they shelled all the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other villages that were known Bellopoje, Tavre [phoen] these are points where the army were with their artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pausing there, you mentioned Suka Bitesh. Can you tell us when, from what period to what period, there were forces stationed at Suka Bitesh?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suka Bitesh, after the Gllogjan attack was captured by the Serb forces, so immediately after March they were stationed there, there was a settlement with houses there, and they allegedly went there to protect the Serb population living in the area. Behind Suka Baballoq there were some Roma people -- houses. They stayed there as well. This is after March. The attack occurred in March, and then after that they were stationed in the Suka.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you help us a little bit more -- in a little more detail about an answer you gave us on page 50, line 5, when you said "they were all along the dam." I just want to understand where that dam is in relation to Lake Radoniq.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the direction of Gjakove, the lower villages --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can't see it in the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Radoniq Lake, so they control all the area around the lake. The road was open to them and they had the vehicles to circulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in your witness statement at paragraph 48 you also make reference, and we've heard some other evidence about this, to the fact that the Serb police station at Qallapek remained open up until the 25th of June. I think you say June. We've heard evidence from another witness putting it on -- as the 25th of June. Do you recall -- is that correct, was the Serb police station in Qallapek open and operating until the second half of June?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was open in June as a police station. They also had tanks. No police force in the world has tanks. The Serb forces were there around the station and in private Albanian homes. There were four tanks, as a matter of fact, above the station. There is a small hill there, and from the hill they also shot against anything that moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do I have it correct, Qallapek is the town that appears in the upper right-hand quadrant of the blue area that you've marked, is that correct, immediately above Kosuriq?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so does it follow --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosuriq and Rosuje between those two is Qallapek and on the road from Qallapek to Kosuriq, there's where the police station was and where the forces were stationed, also in some of the houses in the area and from where they attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so does it follow from the evidence that you've given that there were, if I can summarize it, heavily armed Serb police units moving in and out of that area up until the second half of June?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up until that time they circulated through Rosuje, Kliqine, and Rosuje. They also had tanks and APCs, and that's how changed their forces when they took turns. They always had tanks and APCs to bring their forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm asking you these questions because there are certain passages in your statement that appear to suggest that these areas were under exclusive KLA control, and I know you've given some evidence about that. Can I just briefly recap with you looking at this area that's marked in blue and ask you to confirm, please, that between the 19th and 21st of May there was a Serb offensive approaching into that area from the eastern side in which Grabanica and the villages around that were taken?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's a mistake here. I did not say "controlled by," but that it was considered as a free zone. It's a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you about that in a moment. Then the 29th of May, you've told us about the attacks on Vranoc, and is it right that that was an attack launched in a south-westerly direction from Peje in which there was substantial amount of damage and a substantial amount of people killed in a number of villages along that trajectory?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. On the 29th of May there was a major offensive from the village of Vranoc towards Kryshec, Strellc, towards Decan and up to Junik. But the offensive was prepared professionally by them. They had their tank units, and on the night of the 28th of May, the tank unit approached Vranoc, and the other units captured the strategic points, higher points. And at 5.00 in the morning, the sniper unit and the police unit captured Glavice e Vranocit, that's a hill. A guard was there, he was an elderly person, and two young men were with him as well --.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Forgive me because I'm not going to ask you at this stage about the battle of Vranoc. You've told us about that particular offensive. You've agreed, I think, that there was a major battle over a period of days in the area of Loxha in the first week or at the end of the first week of July. You agree, I think, that there was a major offensive right through the region at the end of July and into the middle of August with Gllogjan being taken on the 11th and 12th of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and then a further offensive at the end of August and into September?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was the largest offensive, but if we return to the Vranoc village that I mentioned earlier, four people were killed and also animals were killed, about 450 heads of domestic animals. Four people were killed, as I said, and many houses were razed to the ground and burnt. Same thing started in Loxha --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment. You told us there was a time when you went to Gllogjan and were -- where the village was under siege and about to be overrun by the Serbs, and Ramush directed you to assist with defences in Gramaqel. Was that on the first August offensive in Gllogjan, on the 11th/12th period; or was it in the second offensive at the end of August/beginning of September?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the first offensive when Gllogjan fell. This was one of the major offensives, and I went there and I did the things that I've already said. And together with my unit I went towards Gramaqel --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- The question that was asked was --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, just pause there for a moment. When you went to Gllogjan, was the battle already well underway?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had started, and the shelling was going on non-stop. They were shelling against the houses --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were grenades, there were rockets falling --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you and cut-off the detail. It's -- there's specific reasons why I'm asking you this question. Is it right then that you did not arrive there on the first day of the Serb offensive against Gllogjan but on the second day?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did not go there the first day. I arrived there the second day, I mean Gllogjan, and it was horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've had an opportunity to look at some of the statements very, very briefly in connection with the Sanije Balaj investigation. And I'm not going to, as I said earlier on, ask you a great many questions about that. But the date on which she is said to have been arrested or detained is given by her relative as the 11th of August. And I just want to ask you: Did you leave that interview with Sanije Balaj and go straight to Gllogjan, where the battle was already raging?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not go that day. I only left her that day, and I don't know where she went. The next day I went to Gllogjan and the offensive was raging, the shelling was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So piecing those chronological factors together, the day that Sanije Balaj left Baran there was a Serb offensive entering Gllogjan. Is that your understanding of the position?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I would put it, but for us there was shelling almost every day. Those days the shelling was more intensive, so much so that we didn't even think of looking at something else or doing something else. We just wanted to go and help people who needed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. One point of clarification on your statement, if I may, on a slightly different topic. Paragraph 77 you refer to the battle of Loxha as having taken place on the 6th of June, 1998. And at paragraph 78 you explained that those taking part included Nazif Ramabaja, Tahir Zemaj, and Ramush Haradinaj. And then at paragraph 9 -- 79 you say: "One month later, in July, the Serbs entered Loxha and destroyed it completely." And you then produce a map which I think Mr. Re made reference to yesterday, which is said to relate to the first battle of Loxha. Now, the date in paragraph 77 I'm going to suggest to you must be wrong and that it's not the 6th of June but the 6th of July, because if you're right in paragraph 78, that Tahir Zemaj and Nazif Ramabaja took part in that conflict, then they of course hadn't entered Kosovo until the 23rd of -- or 24th of June, had they?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the date may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So then does it lead on from that that there was the first battle of Loxha at the end of the first week of July, and then a further battle in Loxha in which it was destroyed completely about a month after that, sometime at the beginning of August? Is that the effect of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is as you say. This happened during the first offensive where all of us took place; in the second one we didn't manage to participate, all of us, in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just two or three more topics, if I may. In the evidence that you gave yesterday - and this is the point that you were just raising a moment ago about control and free zones - you were asked about the blue area that is shown on the map on the screen in front of us. And you were asked whether that was a free area and whether the KLA controlled it militarily. And your response was this: "This is how we considered at that time. We considered it was a free area. They also, the Serbian forces, could enter this area sometimes because they had the people and the vehicles, but we moved around those areas. They, the Serbs, could also move into these areas if they wanted to." And then a little later on you said this: "Yes, this is the map of the villages. These are the villages. However, we could not have them -- we could not have them under our control. We could not prevent everyone to enter into these areas." Can I ask you, please, apart from the major offensives that we've been describing, were there occasions when Serb forces, police or paramilitary, entered into this area in smaller numbers for raids and attacks?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here, during all the time they shelled and tried to enter. For example, Lybeniq village, they attacked the locals who thought that their Serbian neighbours would defend them; but unfortunately, many civilians suffered from that. Almost every day, groups of them tried to enter, killing civilians in various areas, which were closer to them along the main road. Wherever they went, they fired and shelled and killed civilians. So it was, indeed, impossible for us to cover up all that area. We didn't have enough forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to then ask you one or two questions about the incident that was described in relation to Nurije and Istref Krasniqi, which you gave evidence about yesterday. You were asked about rumours that you had heard of a possibility of collaboration, and in the course of answering those questions you said: "I knew that one of the sons was injured. We provided assistance. We took the son to the military hospital to get treatment." Can I ask you this: Were you aware that the son who you had taken to the military hospital to get treatment had been injured as a result of a blood-feud?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know this, but I heard of it later. I heard that he was injured. Then we took him to the military hospital. We didn't dare take him to Peje. We offered him assistance with whatever means we could have, and this is what I know. But I heard from hearsay. We offered assistance, help, to him, and his family visited him in our military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if we could go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn to private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would like to do is pose three or four short questions to this witness on the Sanije Balaj incident, and I don't want by doing so to imply that I have begun to assimilate or approach the material that needs to be read. But there are one or two foundational questions that I can put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has been clear earlier that the mere fact that you're putting some questions in this context does not deprive you from applying later on to a recall of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one or two specific questions. Do you remember when the red Golf vehicle drove away whether Galani was in the car as well?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it. I was walking towards a kiosk near the ambulance, the clinic of the village. And I saw Sanije Balaj entering and them entering the car. There is -- there was a trial in Peje and it was over. I don't remember the exact time. I think it was in the morning about midday, I would say, 1.00 or 2.00. That was the break for the army to have lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment. The simple question I'm asking is: When she got into the vehicle with your cousins, was Galani with them or in the vehicle or not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But did you, in fact, see them get into the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw those two persons and her, I mean Sanije. She was wearing a long coat, and out of curiosity I turned my head thinking that someone might call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So you did see your cousins get into the vehicle with her; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that Galani was not there or that you don't know one way or the other whether he was with them at that time?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I declared also in the other trial, and I'm telling you now, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Second question, please: Sanije Balaj, was she a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw a video-clip in which there was a group of girls singing, it was near Malisheve, and she was one of them, but I don't know. When she came to us she was in civilian clothes, and I didn't have any information to that effect; namely, that she was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just pause there. You say: "I saw a video-clip in which there was a group of girls singing ..." Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, not all of them had the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Were they singing KLA songs or songs that associated them with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were singing a song devoted to the KLA. You could see in that video-clip, they were coming down a mountain, but I didn't know that she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was this a video you saw before you met her in Baran or after?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That video-clip I saw, even though I saw it earlier -- but at that moment I did know it was she, namely, Sanije Balaj. It was just a group of girls that I didn't pay any attention to. Then after that I realised that she was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And then finally this: Have you learnt from anybody at any time subsequently whether she was a member of the KLA or not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't told that because people thought that since I interrogated her I would be the person to have given the order for execution. So if I showed some interest, people might start becoming suspicious, you know, of me because of this belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that and it may, indeed, provide the answer to my last series of questions. When Rrustem Tetaj gave evidence in this court about the investigation that took place into the disappearance of Sanije Balaj, he testified that all of the commanders, including himself, Tahir Zemaj, Gani Gjukaj, and Ramush Haradinaj held at least one meeting in which they were trying to get to the bottom of what had happened to her and were conducting collectively investigations into her death. Did you know that all of the commanders were showing an interest in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. They called me to go to that interview. Each and every one were interested to know what happened, why it happened. The commanders weren't informed of what happened, and normally someone entrusts you with a job, you should take care to know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you go and speak to the commanders together?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because I wasn't there, and then I went to that interview that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And rumours broke out, various rumours. As you know, rumours spread very fast. Then I heard very bad words about myself, as if I was the one who ordered her to be killed. And because of that, I kept a very low profile, not to prevent the investigation and everything, and I wanted the case to be investigated and tried to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's as far as I can take it at this stage with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Could I inquire with other Defence counsel how much time they think they would need. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe I'm going to be a half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I would estimate approximately 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would bring us close to 7.00. Mr. Re, as matters stand now, how much time, if any time at all, you would need for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As matters stand now, possibly ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Troop, would it be able for you to stay on that side of 30 minutes which is closer to 20 than to 40?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'll endeavour to do the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear. Just perhaps some guidance not -- Mr. Emmerson, when you asked the witness whether he went on the same day to assist in defending the attack against Gllogjan, whether that was the same day when he left Sanije Balaj, yes or no, and he said no it's the following day. And then you, for unknown reasons to me, you put it again in chronological order; that is, that it was the day after he left Sanije Balaj, that there was an attack on Gllogjan, which was already so obvious from the previous testimony that I even got the impression that you wanted to emphasise that this was the case rather -- and you really --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- confused the witness there, because he had no idea what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise for that. I must have lost the train of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we stand adjourned until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you may proceed. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith, who's counsel for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to start with a couple of questions dealing with general issues. During the time that you were being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, were you shown any photo-spreads?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us how many photo-spreads you were shown?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall when you were shown those photo-spreads?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was once in Peje when I was shown some photos, and then in Pristina. I remember two places. I think it was sometime in 2002 and at a later time, 2004, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As you sit here today, if you can be of any help, do you by any chance recall who were the individuals or the investigators who showed you those photo-spreads? If you can, that's fine; if you can't, it's understood. It's been some time ago.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Romanian lady with a French guy. I think the name of the French guy was Rene, at least this is what I remember. They showed me photographs. There was a Czech guy and Shahzada Sultan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the witness now used the word "photo" and "photograph" twice whereas you asked about photo-spreads. Can you ensure that there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Following up on the Judge's question you indicated -- you said that you were shown photos. When I say a photo-spread what I'm referring to is a sheet of paper on which there were a number of different photographs of people, sometimes perhaps eight. That's what I'm referring to when I use the term "photo-spread."

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this very well. Now I am clear about question. Yes, they showed me a photo-spread with various photos, out of which I recognised three persons, two by name, and one only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were being shown those photo-spreads, did you sign -- after you recognised the two by name, did you sign a document and then give it to any of the investigators or the people that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall one of the investigators who showed you a photo-spread that you signed was the gentleman that you named, Sultan, I think it's -- I'm sorry, it's a woman, Shahzada Sultan?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this person. I know that it's a man, actually, not a woman, and is from Pakistani and works here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll make further inquiries about this issue someplace else. During the time that you were giving statements to the investigators, do you recall if you were ever audiotaped or videotaped?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time I was called for an interview, they informed me that it was being audiotaped, but this didn't prevent me in any way. I was told that it was being recorded. And they asked me whether I had any problems if it was recorded; I said, okay, I don't have a problem. But I don't know where it was actual recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were never shown a transcript of any audiotapes of any interviews that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor, were you?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember to have been shown any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to another issue which is when you first took over responsibility for training the young men that you've testified about, could you tell us what colour, if there was a colour; or what uniforms, if there were uniforms, that those young men wore?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was February, end of February/beginning of March, and there were almost no uniforms. All of us were dressed in civilian clothes, and with some KLA patches on the arm, you know, because we didn't have any real uniforms. We had civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time when some people started wearing black clothes as a kind of uniform with a KLA patch during the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this was the first time we saw uniforms in Malisheve, and we heard that it was the military police that wore this uniform. Some individuals purchased uniforms with their own money; those who couldn't afford didn't have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the individuals who were wearing black uniforms, were those such people as Mete Krasniqi, Fadil Nimoni, for example?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mete didn't have for a while, but then he bought the uniform in Malisheve. Once Fadil didn't have uniform, but a time came when he did buy the uniform. So at the beginning they didn't, but later they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By -- when you say "later they did," could you help us out and give us a month or a period of time in which that occurred. Would that have been by June or July?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that it was summer and I know that in Malisheve they started wearing uniforms earlier, but I don't think it was of any importance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What about in Baran? In Baran did people wear -- did soldiers wear black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Baran there were some who had uniforms but not every one of them. They also bought the uniforms with their own money, and the people who we thought would serve in the police unit had similar uniform, the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by saying "people who served in the police unit," those would be people such as Avni, your cousin; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they bought the uniforms and they wished to serve in the military police. It was their wish to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Iber, he was another individual who wore a black uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think he had such uniforms. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in the area where you were stationed, there were also civilians who wore black clothing in support of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. There were people in our area who wore those clothes. They thought they seemed more interesting if they wore such clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by "interesting," it was also an indication of support for the UCK and for the fight against the Serbs; true?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their aim, to express their support for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you are aware that these questions are of a rather general nature and that the answers are of a similar general nature --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do appreciate this. Unfortunately I don't have civilians about me, and all I can do is give this information to the Chamber to use as it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time it's general, very general.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you first were approached by Avni and Iber, your cousins, concerning Sanije Balaj, you were in the presence of Nazif Ramabaja; right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, he is the person who told you that it would be appropriate for you to talk to her about the concerns that your cousins had raised; right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you went to go speak with her, initially you were talking to her in a room where there were your two cousins and somebody you later learned was Galani; true?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So there was Sanije and that person and then myself and my two cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you first saw her, as you were discussing with Mr. Emmerson a few minutes ago, you were surprised because she -- you thought she was a member of our army, and you had seen her in a video wearing a UCK uniform singing patriotic songs; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. There was a video-recording where she was featuring in that video, but I don't know whether she was a regular member or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was information, as a matter of fact, that you gave to the Prosecution in your first statement in March of 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And referring the Court and counsel to paragraph 12 of the statement of 5 March 2006, the ERN number is U0094451.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, after you spoke with her, you were satisfied, based upon your conversation with her and the information that you reviewed, that it was okay for her to be released; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After, or rather, because I did not have the possibility to speak longer to her, then I told her to go to her own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, you told Galani, Avni Krasniqi, and Iber Krasniqi of your conclusion regarding the fact that she could be released and go to her own house, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you told those gentlemen of your conclusion, you went back to your commander, Nazif Ramabaja, and you told him the whole story and he said to you that you had done a good job by releasing the woman; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After that, your next real involvement with the questions about what had happened to Sanije Balaj was when you went to the inquiry where you made the statement that you made in Prapaqan, where the commanders were all present and interested in what had happened; true?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because this issue had come up, people were speaking about her and people wanted to know what happened to her. Her family wanted to know what happened to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the Chamber is not united yet on whether it's 70 per cent or 80 per cent repetitious, the evidence you are eliciting from the witness at this moment. Almost everything that he answered now he has been -- he has said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you were involved in that inquiry, you had no further -- well, let me put it to you this way. I'm going to read something to you and I'm going to ask you, when I finish reading this to you, whether you have any comment on this. And this comes from the statement of Shaban Balaj, which is dated the 15th of October, 2002, and I received in the supporting materials for the amendments to the proposed third indictment and it's statement number 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph would be, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It would be on -- unfortunately it's not -- the end of paragraph four, it would be U0030892 at the top of the page -- it would be paragraph -- page 3 of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- and in terms of the document itself, it's page 20.159. This is the statement of Shaban Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "I reported the incident to Commander Tahir Zemaj, Hasan Gashi became the main investigator, Fadil Nimoni. Fadil is dead but Hasan Gashi still lives in Peje. Hasan and Fadil started investigating the case and I went to Prapaqan every day to get progress. They questioned soldiers involved, and on the sixth day I was given the official information that my sister had been killed. I also received a statement saying that she had done nothing illegal. "I gathered together some 20 men of my family and we went to the house of Mete Krasniqi in Vranoc. We got inside and we met the brother of Mete's. I don't know his name. We told him why we came, and he said Mete was not at home, and he didn't know where Avni was. "We asked for the commander of their group who was Din Krasniqi and also a member of the same family. Din arrived at the house and greeted us. The oldest member of our family," I turn to the next page, "Shaqir Balaj started discussing the issue with Din on behalf of our family. Shaqir asked where Sanije Balaj was and said he wants to have an answer before the next morning" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, your speed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "When we left we saw Mete coming together with someone else. We went to speak to him and got into an argument. Mete said that he didn't kill Sanije, but he couldn't guarantee anything about Avni and Idriz. Shaqir told Mete to bring Sanije home to our" -- excuse me, "to our home dead or alive by the evening or something bad would happen. "After this, we left and we went to Strellc to wait. We stayed at home, but nothing happened. Three days later, the imam of Vranoc, nowadays imam of Drenica, came to the house of Shaqir, together with Mete Krasniqi, Ramadan Gashi, my nephew, Zeqir Gjoci, another nephew, and Xhavit Uka another friend of my nephew. All of the men, approximately 50 persons from the Balaj family, were invited to Saqir's house. A discussion started and Mete again said he didn't have a murder on his conscience, but that he couldn't guarantee for Avni Krasniqi and Idriz Gashi, also known as Galani. He said that Galani killed Sanije by shooting and Avni was with him. Shaqir told Mete that he had done the wrong thing by stopping Sanije, knowing who she was, but that he is clean, considering the murder. That was the end of the meeting." Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have any awareness of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I was not there myself and I don't know what they talked about. Because, as I told you, I was not present there. I didn't even ask what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when Shaban Balaj says: "Shaqir, who was the head of the family, told Mete that he had done the wrong thing by stopping Sanije, knowing who she was, but that he is clean considering the murder," would it be fair to say that that was a kind of trial for Mete as to whether or not he was guilty of that murder?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are different circumstances in our part of the world the way things are done there are different, and the family who has somebody taken from them and don't know about their fate have the right to do that. However, this is his statement. He's been present there. He knows what he's talking about. I was not there. I don't think it was a trial. This was a traditional way of solving this. The village and the family wanted to know about the fate of one of their member and wanted to ask why that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is the fact that Shaqir stated that he is clean considering the murder such that there is no blood debt that would be owed by Mete Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe there's a mistake here. From what I understand, what was said there is that Mete had not committed the murder. And then the statement says that Galan committed the murder, but Avni was with him; this is what I understood. And maybe -- probably Shaqir alluded that he was present there with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Based upon your conversation with Sanije, I'd like to know whether you could comment on this part of Shaban Balaj's statement which would be page 5, Your Honours and Mr. Re. "I cannot think of any other reason for what happened to Sanije than money. She had 2.000 Deutschemarks with her when she left home for Peje. I think the suspects would have only taken the money and let her go, but they couldn't because they knew they would get caught."

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whose statement this is, Shaban's statement or somebody else's, but this is not something I said. I don't know who said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based on the information that you had after you spoke with her, does that seem like a reasonable possibility why Sanije was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I object to the question. There's absolutely no foundation for Mr. Guy-Smith to put it in that form without leading up to it with a lot more foundational questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I understood your testimony correctly, you've been a police officer for some period of time, have you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the reason that you were chosen by your commander Ramabaja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm going to stop you here. The witness has testified as to what was the subject of the conversation. You're asking him now on the basis of the conversation whether this could be a reasonable explanation, that calls for inferences at a level, unless there would be something else in the conversation which has not been established yet. Because I understand from the conversation that the witness did not find any reason to believe that there was collaboration. Okay. Then all other reasons in the world are open to do something to another person --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Except for the fact that he did find a substantial sum of money about her person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that -- so it's not all other reasons and that's where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then if that's the case, don't you think that the Chamber could understand if someone has a considerable amount of money, that that could be a reason to attack a person? I mean whether -- if the witness would say, No, no, it could not possibly be if someone has a huge amount of money with them could not possibly be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the Chamber is satisfied that that is a reasonable alternative explanation for the murder of Sanije Balaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just as reasonable as many others, but reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Reasonable, that's all I care about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber considers that this could explain, just as many other matters could explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to a couple of issues concerning this statement you made which has been called your 92 ter statement, and I'm not going to go over that which you said in great detail; but I would like to talk to you about two specific issues, if I might. You said that you -- in your statement that you heard about Togeri for the first time in May of 1998 and that you met him briefly as he was travelling on his way to Pozhare. And my question is this: In your 92 ter statement it says, and I'm at paragraph 60, the very last line, and I'm moving to the last page: "He looked rather weak." In a previous statement which is a statement you gave on January 7th and 9th of 2007, paragraph 61, you said: "He looked rather ill." Is your impression of how he looked the same - and by that I mean he looked sickly to you and at that point he didn't look particularly well, he looked weak. Is that what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes, he was much thinner than today, not only him. All of us were much thinner and looked much paler.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And finally I'd like to refer to -- finally I'd like to refer to paragraph 81 of your statement and paragraph 76 of the second statement of Cufe Krasniqi, which is dated January 7th and 9th. And I'd like to ask you about the following. In your statement dated January 7th and 9th you say the following on paragraph 76, page 13 of 17: "I heard that the detainee allegedly said he wanted to be a member of the KLA with his family. As he received the permission from Ramush Haradinaj and Togeri to move freely in the area, he entered a house by force in an Albanian house in the village Klina with the Serbian police." And here's my question to you, sir: In the 92 ter statement, the statement that we have before us, in paragraph 81, there is the following said with regard to who he received permission from. It says: "As he received the permission from Ramush to move freely in the area," and the two words that I saw in your statement of January 9th, "and Togeri," are missing. Is the statement that you made on January 7th and 9th which reads as follows: "As he received the permission from Ramush Haradinaj and Togeri" accurate?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about Sali Shkreli now who was a collaborator of the Serbs, together with his family, and he was interrogated. After the police withdrew from the Qallapek station, Sali expressed his wish to become a member of the KLA to protect his own village. He came and said that Ramush, Toger, and whoever else was with them, they had said that he was free to move in the area. I did not see that piece of paper. He told me that he had been left free to move around in the area. I did not see any piece of paper. Soldiers also told me that he had been given permission to move freely; however, who gave him that permission, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But the information that you've given us was that he was given permission to move around the area by most Ramush Haradinaj and Togeri; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and then I thought if they gave him the permission to move freely in the area, he came to the village of Kosuriq and I thought that we must accept him. This is a person who wants to be with us, and better with us than against us. But during the time, the short time that he stayed with us, he went to the police station in Kliqine. There was a young man together with his wife living in a house close by, and he expelled them from the house and lived there with his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Krasniqi. The thrust of my question dealt with the issue of who gave him permission, and you have answered that question, that the permission came from both Haradinaj and Togeri. And I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said that I would do my best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- to stay within the time and I'm six minutes over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one doubts that you did your best, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, time is short, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi, I represent Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: In March 1998 you were in Jablanica with Dr. Din Krasniqi. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And Dr. Din Krasniqi was meeting Lahi Brahimaj. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You were also in attendance; correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: In 1998, that was the only work meeting that you were present at with Lahi Brahimaj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went there with Din, so I met him in Jabllanice. That was the first meeting in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you had no other work meetings with Lahi Brahimaj in 1998, did you?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later we met, but the first time I met him was there. I think we also met once or twice in Baran on the way going somewhere, we also met in Vranoc, so two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And I believe you may also met whilst you were fighting sometime in September 1998. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was the time of the September offensive, and I met him. That was a terrible offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And in 1998, do you remember how many times you went to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I didn't need to remember those things. Whenever I needed something, a vehicle or something else, I would go there. But that does not mean that I met Lahi Brahimaj every time I went there. Sometimes he would come to my area and he would not find me, he would find somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Could we bring up document number 65 ter 1099, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like you to -- I'd like to ask you some questions about the staff headquarters that you briefly described in Jablanica. And the first question I'd like to ask is for you to confirm that the building was at the entry to the village on the left-hand side as you approach from Zhabel village. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. The doors were wooden door, but I would look at it from another angle, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: This photograph that is on the screen should show the view of the KLA staff as you approach from Zhabel village. Do you remember this view?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And I think you said that you recall it being used as a kitchen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right. There was another facility before that, I think. What I see here was a kitchen --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- used for eating, you know, and cooking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'll show you another view in a minute, but what I'd like to ask you about is that this -- or these two buildings were in the middle of a meadow. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was a meadow between them, and they were also surrounded by a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And unlike many Albanian houses that have a wall all around the compound, the meadow didn't have a wall around it. I think we can see just a small fence on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Whoever can afford it can have a wall built around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: In this case the buildings and the meadow were used for grazing animals, so it was not necessary, was it, to construct a wall around the meadow?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us it has no significance. Whoever can afford it can construct a wall. There are many houses like the one I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Could -- Your Honour, could that be tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be D117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection, Mr. Re? D117 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Could we now bring up 65 ter document 1104, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You were aware, were you not, Mr. Krasniqi, that this building was where soldiers slept in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I saw soldiers eating there and staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: This shows a view from the meadow towards the two buildings. Does that accord with your recollection of the two buildings you've previously described?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It's a nice view of them. You can see the forest and the meadow. You can see the door -- the gate and you can see that they are wooden gates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you can also see that on the left-hand side between the next property or the second in the village, the wall only extends a short distance from the entrance gate?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the wall, and from that you can guess that the person, the owner, couldn't afford to build to have the wall surround the entire property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, sorry to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I -- please go ahead, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you clarify if this meadow was used for grazing animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, could you just confirm that the meadow shown in the foreground of the photograph was the one which you described as being used for grazing animals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think you, Mr. Troop, gave this description, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the meadow is used for grazing animals. The cows grazed there. The grass is eaten by cows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to ask you about Lahi Brahimaj. You knew that Lahi Brahimaj or the Brahimaj family were from Jablanica, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They were from Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And also, you've said that Jablanica, because of its particular geographic location was very favourable to defend from an encroachment by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a village, a mountainous village, not a big one. Bishtrica of Decan runs nearby. There aren't many houses and inhabitants in it. It's just a mountainous zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can I ask you whether, Mr. Krasniqi, in 1998 you were area that the KLA had a so-called General Staff?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't refer to it as a General Staff. There were some soldiers, but I think a General Staff would be something else. We tried to have a General Staff, but as I said earlier in our case every village had a staff. And maybe this creates confusion among people whom I think that every village has its own staff, has its own army, fighting against an army belonging to a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Krasniqi, that's why I refer to it as a "so-called General Staff." The question was: Were you aware of an organisation calling itself the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the Serbian forces couldn't enter that area for a long time, and it was a very nice thing to see because there were no police patrols there, nobody was maltreated and so on. But if people left that village and went to other places, whenever they were captured, detained -- they were detained, they were maltreated, and so this was left as a pretext, I would say, for these people. They were left alone in the area, but once they left that area, they were of course beaten up and maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd like to move away from Jablanica and even away from the so-called Dukagjin Zone. Were you aware of another organisation which was the KLA General Staff, unrelated from these zones? It may be that you were not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we were not informed. We were not aware of any General Staff because there weren't genuine structures that effect. If we had, we would have been very lucky, but we didn't. There wasn't any such General Staff on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Would it, therefore, come as a surprise to you to learn if I told you that Lahi Brahimaj was on the so-called General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I'm not aware of something, I wouldn't be surprised at things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: But you didn't know that during 1998, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Witness has answered that question, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: It was just the question of the time as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said at the time. He put it in a time-frame. "At that time, we were not informed," he said and I understood that as reference to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. Before we move on, perhaps I can ask for that photograph to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Re, then D118 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And if you didn't know about the General Staff, you would not have known where it was located nor what Lahi Brahimaj's responsibilities were within the General Staff, would you?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And for your information, and as background to the questions which I'm going to ask you, I'm just going to tell you that it's our case that Lahi Brahimaj's responsibilities included logistics and finance, and in particular the distribution of weapons across the different zones. Do you follow that?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was in Jabllanice and that when villagers went up to him to ask for assistance, he helped them. He even gave them weapons. He escorted unarmed young men to the mountains to go to Albania to get weapons and come back. So two, three had weapons. A great majority of young people didn't, so they had to go through the mountains to find weapons, trying to avoid the Serbian forces. Some of them fell in ambushes and were killed on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: One of the main things that Lahi Brahimaj was known for was the ability to procure weapons, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And that was weapons not just for Jablanica but for other areas as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the other areas went to him for assistance because it's very difficult for one to cross the border and to walk in that terrain without knowing the place. So close to him there were people who knew the terrain and they helped such people who wanted weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You explained to us that in early 1998 each village created a so-called headquarters or staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right that each village had its own commander and took care of supplies they needed, including weapons and other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And I think you've also said that each village did not have authority over the next village?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If a village has its own command, it has its own logistics and there are some documents which I don't see here, but in those documents you can see the Gllogjan village -- Naberxhan not Gllogjan and Kosuriq and Kryshec village which were captured by the Serbian forces and in that document it says the quantity of weapons and what they had. There is another document I signed which speaks about Naberxhan village and the weapons we gave to them and how many weapons we gave to them. Everything happened on a voluntary basis. People came to us on a voluntary basis and asked from things and we gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Following on from your answer, as the villages got organised, the most important thing which they needed and the primary thing which they needed was weapons, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that moment, yes. One would give anything just to have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You've explained, I think, in paragraphs 30 and 31 of your statement that in February your relatives, Din Krasniqi and his cousin Mete -- no, sent his cousin Mete Krasniqi to your house in February 1998?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mete came. He was sent by Din, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And at that stage it was agreed that Din Krasniqi was going to be -- Dr. Din Krasniqi was going to be the commander for the Baran area, Baran valley?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time he was the commander of Vranoc village alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: But there had already been an agreement that he was the commander for that area by February 1998, was there not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before February 1998, after February, and in March the battle took place in Vranoc village and then this happened after the attack on Vranoc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me a moment. At paragraph 31 of your statement you say -- this was -- or first you say: "In February 1998 Din Krasniqi sent his cousin Mete Krasniqi to my house." And then at paragraph 31 -- would you like to just look at paragraph 30 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The word "later" seems to create problems which I would not mind if you would have explored them, but the way of questioning is certainly not resolving the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No, I thought I'd start again from paragraph 30 Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: So can you see that in paragraph 30 you describe that in February 1998 Mete Krasniqi came to your house. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And then can you look at paragraph 31 of your statement, please?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you can see at the first paragraph it says: "From that day, I started training the UCK soldiers." That refers to February 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This refers to 1998. On that day I agreed to go and talk with Din, and from that day we -- it was decided that I train the soldiers. On the next day, the soldiers came voluntarily and there was a number of them. And we started training them on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And then still on paragraph 31 of your statement you say: "At that time Dr. Din Krasniqi was the UCK commander for Vranoc and later for the Baran valley." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned it even earlier, that this happened at a later time. That is correct. The first time he was responsible only for Vranoc, but on account of his growing authority then we decided that he would be responsible for the Baran valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: When Dr. Din Krasniqi and Lahi Brahimaj met in March 1998 in Jablanica, Dr. Din Krasniqi had some authority and he had some agreement that he was going to act as a representative of the Vranoc village or the Vranoc area by that time, had he not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The village or the area, Mr. Troop. If you put a question with two different propositions it might be difficult for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: For Vranoc.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was responsible for the -- only for the village. Because after the war in Drenice, then the war spread in Dukagjin in our area. There were injured soldiers in Jabllanice. Din was a doctor, and of course he visited, not only the soldiers but also the civilians. He was a very good doctor the people loved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, I'm looking at the clock. It's 7.00. We can do two things, take our time and then continue on Monday, or try to finish, but then first of all with the assistance of interpreters, transcribers, technicians, but then we really have to finish within the next 10 to 12 minutes I would say if we get approval. That would mean that since Mr. Re would need some time as well Mr. Re would have ten minutes. Can you finish in two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I cannot, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, the Chamber expects you to finish in three or four minutes. This decision is also based on the way you used the time. If you ask for the necessity of a wall around a meadow, why not just draw our attention to the fact that you -- by it seems at least that you want to establish that through all these questions this Chamber might think that it would not have been a real prison. That's really not -- you underestimate I think the ability of the Chamber to understand situations. You have four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have got four minutes left, Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I don't think I can finish in four minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to do your best in four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when Din Krasniqi met with Lahi Brahimaj, the main reason for the meeting was to source weapons for Vranoc, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First he was supposed to check on some injured people and sick people, and then he would talk with them about weapons. This is the accurate version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
